summary: Washoe County summit lookout built in 1942 on Peavine Mountain; abandoned by 1964 and gone, removal date unknown; radio towers on the summit today.

facts.design: Standard 14-by-14-foot lookout building with sleeping quarters, moved from a Susanville site
facts.status_note: Abandoned in 1964 and still standing in 1972; the 2012 report says it is no longer standing and does not know when it was removed
facts.agency: Mono National Forest with the Grazing Service (1942)

access.note: Public land with trails; access from northwest Reno has become more restricted

visit.trail_note: Hiking and mountain bike trails cross the mountain; a road serves the radio sites on the summit

events.note: Lookout placed on the summit under a joint Mono forest and Grazing Service project; the building came from a Susanville site
Station placed in operation July 21, 1942; J.P. Ryan of the Mono forest assigned to the post

evidence.supports: work began April 1942 on a standard lookout on the summit
evidence.quote: active work is under way on a project to build a standard type of fire lookout station on the summit of Peavine.

evidence.supports: joint project of the Mono forest and the Grazing Service
evidence.quote: The project is one of collaboration between the Mono national forest and Region 3 of the grazing service.

evidence.supports: Forest Service supplied a standard 14-by-14-foot building with sleeping quarters
evidence.quote: The forest service is to supply a standard size 14'x14' lookout building, equipped with sleeping quarters and facilities.

evidence.supports: Grazing Service supplied workers, supervision and engineering plans
evidence.quote: The grazing service is supplying the manpower and supervision, as well as preparing engineering plans.

evidence.supports: building came from a Susanville site where it was not in use
evidence.quote: A building owned by the forest service, and not in use, has been dismantled, and moved from the Susanville section

evidence.supports: planned five-mile road from U.S. Highway 395 to the station
evidence.quote: a road must be constructed five miles in length, from U.S. Highway 395

evidence.supports: Grazing Service completed a truck trail to the station by June 1942
evidence.quote: has just completed construction of a truck trail to the station

evidence.supports: station placed in operation July 21, 1942 through the Mono forest and grazing division
evidence.quote: The fire lookout station atop Peavine mountain, northwest of Reno, was placed in operation today through the joint efforts of the Mono national forest service and the division of grazing.

evidence.supports: J.P. Ryan of the Mono forest assigned to the post for the summer season
evidence.quote: with J.P. Ryan of the Mono forest service being assigned to the post.

evidence.supports: 2012 report says the Tahoe NF built it originally
evidence.quote: Built originally by Tahoe NF, later staffed by Nevada Division
then abandoned in 1964 - was still standing in 1972.
unsure of when it was removed.

evidence.supports: radio towers and transmitters on the summit
evidence.quote: To service and install the radio towers and transmitters located on the peak and on several promontories

evidence.supports: access road winds up the north and east faces
evidence.quote: winding up the north and east faces of the mountain
many miles of hiking and mountain bike trails have been added

evidence.supports: access from northwest Reno increasingly restricted over fifteen years
evidence.quote: access has become increasingly restricted in the past fifteen years from Northwest Reno

sources.title: Peavine Mountain
sources.publisher: Forest Lookouts (West Lookouts site), quoting 1942 Nevada State Journal reports

sources.title: California-Sierra and Nevada Chapter 2012 Annual Report

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The 1942 newspaper items credit the Mono forest and the Grazing Service; the 2012 report says the Tahoe National Forest built it originally. The story reports both.

notes_for_editor: Brief said the lookout was built by the Tahoe NF; the 1942 articles credit the Mono forest and the Grazing Service, so the builder is disputed. The removal date is unknown. The radio sites on the summit come from Wikipedia only. No photos found.
